Yet passing available tests does not establish that an implementation satisfies its natural language specification. Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the specification and scenarios that thoroughly exercise the code, but current benchmarks provide limited insight into whether agents can construct such evidence themselves. We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories, covering 8 types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. Given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising executable checks and test scenarios. The checks should reject implementations that violate the specification while accepting those that satisfy it, and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise the code. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, none constructs a harness scored as faithful on the benchmark's implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The bottleneck lies less in exploring test scenarios than in constructing checks that faithfully reflect the specification. Specifically, the agents show a clear tendency to write checks that mirror the reference implementation rather than the specification, and therefore reject implementations that the specification permits.
triage_reason: Benchmark of whether coding agents write validation harnesses; shares L1's benchmark word, a new static test set with no instrument.

title: Compositional RL: Evaluating and Training LLMs for Collaborative Reasoning
abstract: Language models are often evaluated alone but increasingly deployed together, routed between, made to debate, ensembled, or collaboratively trained. For a model inside a system, what matters most is not how well it performs on its own, but how much the system gains from its presence. We call this a model's compositional strength and formalize it using the Shapley value of a cooperative game over coalitions of a model pool, and use a model's leave-one-out contribution to the full coalition as a tractable proxy, requiring n+1 rather than 2^n system evaluations. Evaluating individual vs. compositional strengths across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, we find them largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method-family) settings, individual strength does not translate into compositional advantages, and the coupling is weakest among general-purpose models that practitioners are most likely to deploy. Standalone benchmarks are therefore often poor proxies for models' value in collaborative systems. We then propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome produced by the system as a whole, rather than the policy's correctness in isolation. The leave-one-out baseline in Shapley values cancels under a group policy gradient, so this needs no additional rollout cost beyond RL on the collaborative system's outcome and never requires running a coalition without the policy. Across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings, lifting collaborative performance by +4.0 to +5.4 pts on average (~3x the gain of baselines), up to +13.1 pts.
triage_reason: Shapley and leave-one-out contribution of a model inside a multi-model system; supplies multi-agent credit neighbor.
positioning_default: lab-contested (lab position only via definitive-comparison or owned-artifact shapes)

title: Efficient Resource-Shiftable RL Post-training with Generative Rewards
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with generative reward models (GenRM) has become a central recipe for improving large language models (LLMs), and it is also increasingly resource-intensive: policy rollout, GenRM-based reward evaluation, and policy training all compete for GPU resources. However, existing colocated and disaggregated systems rely on static resource allocation for these roles. Such allocation cannot adapt as each role's workload changes during RL and therefore leaves a role's resources underutilized. We present PivotRL, an RL post-training system that dynamically shifts resources among different roles according to their runtime demands. PivotRL introduces a resource-shiftable runtime built on a Global Parameter Storage, together with a unified mechanism that efficiently shifts role-specific context. A shift-aware scheduler enables sequence migration upon a shift, while a planner considers the aggregate throughput benefit and the shift overhead to determine when and how to shift. We evaluate PivotRL on a 128-GPU cluster using four model groups spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. PivotRL enables resource shifting within seconds and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.81-2.05 times over colocated deployment and 1.50-1.95 times over disaggregated deployment, while preserving RL convergence.
triage_reason: Async RL post-training system that shifts GPUs between rollout, reward and training roles; direct L3 neighbor.

title: Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.
triage_reason: Prefill-decode disaggregation for multi-turn agentic RL rollout: a rollout-engine systems result for L3.

title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.
triage_reason: Fully asynchronous agentic RL framework on Megatron and SGLang: async RL infrastructure for L3; L2 words only.

title: Neos: Learning to Interleave Search and Visual Reasoning
abstract: Recent multimodal deep search agents have advanced tool use and visual content retrieval, yet they still struggle to convert intermediate visual evidence into actionable guidance for subsequent search, limiting their effectiveness in long-horizon settings. To address this gap, we present Neos, a multimodal deep search framework that learns both how to acquire evidence and how to use it to guide subsequent decisions. To make this coupling learnable, Neos constructs training tasks with intermediate visual dependencies while filtering out textual shortcuts, and introduces a lightweight, trainable Multimodal Evidence Interface (MEI) that transforms retrieved content into goal-conditioned observations. At its core, an agent-environment co-evolution procedure treats MEI as a co-adaptive component of this loop. Specifically, reference-guided credit assignment uses verified successful trajectories to localize critical policy errors while preserving credit for useful decisions in failed searches, whereas rollout feedback selects informative local evidence-processing interactions for MEI supervised fine-tuning (SFT). By alternating policy reinforcement learning (RL) with MEI SFT, Neos allows the policy's evolving evidence requests to shape MEI training and the adapted MEI to reshape subsequent observations, closing the loop between evidence acquisition and evidence-conditioned action. Across ten benchmarks, Neos-9B and Neos-35B demonstrate leading performance among specialized multimodal deep-search agents.
triage_reason: Multimodal search agent with a trained evidence interface; shares L2 training and L4 context words but is a domain recipe.

title: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning
abstract: What information does a reinforcement learning policy omit? At each state, a standard policy stores one probability per action. It has no place to record how actions relate to each other, such as which pairs go together and which conflict. We ask when this missing structure matters, and we give exact answers. We store the policy at each state as a density matrix, a positive semidefinite, unit-trace matrix borrowed from quantum information theory. We use it here as a purely classical data structure, computed on ordinary classical hardware. The diagonal holds the usual action probabilities. The off-diagonal entries, called coherences, are new parameters. This gives density-matrix reinforcement learning (DMRL). Coherences change outcomes in two settings. First, suppose a policy is regularized toward a coherent reference policy using matrix relative entropy. The optimum then has coherences that no diagonal reference policy produces, and its action probabilities can depend on the reference policy's coherences. This is relevant to fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) with a Kullback--Leibler penalty. Second, suppose the agent chooses a unit-vector action and the reward is a quadratic function of that vector. This could arise when an LLM judge scores a weighted consolidation of reasoning paths, or when coupled robotic sensors each respond to a mix of actions. Then some coherent policies earn strictly more expected reward than every classical policy with the same action probabilities, and we give the margin in closed form. In a two-action example, both policies assign probability $0.5$ to each action, yet the classical one earns expected reward $0$ while the coherent one earns $1$, the maximum. Outside these two settings, DMRL matches or transfers the classical results. This is a theory paper. All results are proved, and we report no empirical evaluation.
triage_reason: Density-matrix policy parameterization; shares L2's RL words but no agent, long-horizon or credit question.

title: UMCR: Universal Medical Concept Recognition through Guideline Integration and Agentic Linking
abstract: Medical Concept Recognition is the task of extracting and grounding spans in medical text to entries in a standard ontology. Current methods are generally developed towards a single ontology and source text type (clinical notes, drug labels, etc.) The central challenge is therefore to build methods that adapt to any target ontology without requiring ontology-specific retraining. More recent approaches like REAL and AutoPCR make direct use of Large Language Models and can theoretically adapt to any ontology choice but suffer from a lack of generalization. We propose UMCR, a pipeline that allows extraction and linking to any target ontology using any source text variety, utilizing direct guideline integration and an agentic linking module. We evaluate our method on the recent MedPath benchmark, covering a wide variety of medical text types and vocabularies, and show that our method achieves strong performance across these tasks. This ability unlocks interoperability in the healthcare domain, allowing for extraction and alignment between different medical standards. Our method also reduces dependence on parametric LLM memory, thanks to improved interaction with the target ontology compared to other proposed approaches.
triage_reason: Medical concept recognition pipeline; agentic linking is a domain application with no lane question.

title: Beyond Successful Play: Diagnosing Opponent Modeling in Large Language Models
abstract: Language-model agents are expected to adapt to others whose behavior changes through interaction. Yet adaptation may rely on learned behavioral patterns rather than theory of mind (ToM): the ability to infer others' mental states, including beliefs and intentions. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic framework for repeated hide-and-seek against algorithmic opponents with explicitly defined recursive belief updates. Their ground-truth beliefs and action probabilities let us distinguish adaptive play, action prediction, and belief tracking through live interaction, fixed-history evaluation, and controlled information interventions. With structured elicitation and behavioral supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we find improved play in several tested settings, but diagnostics reveal limitations in opponent prediction and belief tracking. We test whether supervising opponent action probabilities can address this predictive deficit in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Predictions improve when the model is told the opponent's type and parameter settings, but become less accurate when it must infer the opponent from history without this information. Training on examples that also omit these details reduces the gap, although improvements vary across opponents. Is this limitation specific to smaller open-weight models, or does it also appear in a frontier model? GPT-5.4 also benefits from correct opponent beliefs: supplying them improves its predictions and choices, whereas deeper explicit belief reports and self-generated memory do not consistently improve forecasting from interaction history. This contrast suggests that using useful belief information is easier than inferring it autonomously, even for a frontier model. Together, our findings distinguish improved play and action prediction from reliable belief tracking, providing a framework for evaluating mentalizing and testing targeted improvements.
triage_reason: Opponent-modeling diagnostic for LLMs in hide-and-seek; shares L1 measurement words but is a theory-of-mind test, not agent reliability or validity.

title: FunDM: Cheap & Label-Free Decision Models from Frozen Language Models
abstract: Decision models such as Jev score candidate answers or actions. A small decision head trained label-free can recover about 99% of a frozen language model's multiple-choice accuracy while using only two-thirds of its transformer layers. It learns the full model's answer probabilities with KL divergence, without correct-answer labels for training. One backbone pass reads the question and all options together; the head returns probabilities for every option. We call this model FunDM (Fun Decision Model). Using 24 of Qwen3-8B's 36 layers and skipping the LM head, its +1T variant reaches 75.0% mean accuracy over eight benchmarks, versus 75.7% for the full model. On MMLU-Pro, both heads achieve 1.56 to 1.57 times batched vLLM throughput with about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory. Both heads score higher than released Contrastive Language Models (CLM), fine-tuned CLM, and CLM-shaped heads trained from scratch on the eight multiple-choice benchmarks and coding-agent selection. Separately trained agent heads learn judge probabilities without pass/fail labels and select passing runs for 74.4 to 74.6 of 100 held-out tasks on average, versus 74 for the full-model judge and 52.0 for a CLM-shaped action-trained head. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM
triage_reason: Label-free decision head on a frozen LM for multiple-choice; no agent loop, RL or systems question.

title: Glasseek: A Transparent Recipe for Training and Trustworthy Evaluation of DeepSearch Agents
abstract: Deep search enables language agents to solve complex information-seeking tasks through iterative web exploration. However, developing robust open-source agents remains challenging for three reasons. First, opaque trajectory-construction pipelines make training data difficult to audit and reproduce. Second, context compression can create a substantial mismatch between training and inference. Third, agents may retrieve benchmark content from the open web during evaluation, contaminating the results and overstating their performance. To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce Glasseek, a fully transparent deep search framework spanning the complete development lifecycle, releasing all data, model weights, training recipes, and code. Specifically, for data construction, we establish a verifiable trajectory curation pipeline that systematically generates high-quality exploration paths. For training, we propose Compaction-Managed GSPO (CM-GSPO), which uses the same policy for search and summarization while optimizing only execution sub-trajectories, enabling end-to-end search-policy training across context-compaction boundaries. For evaluation, we conduct the first systematic audit of test-set leakage in open-web agents and release a modular anti-leakage plugin that seamlessly integrates into existing evaluation harnesses. Under this rigorous evaluation protocol, our 9B agent outperforms frontier proprietary agents across almost all deep research benchmarks spanning diverse task types, and achieves the best overall performance among recent open-weight agents, setting a new state of the art at the 9B scale.
triage_reason: Open deep-search recipe: benchmark contamination from web retrieval (L1 validity) and train-inference mismatch from context compression (L4).

title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.
triage_reason: Navigation world model with spatial memory; 'memory' is scene representation, shares only L4's word.

title: AuthGateBench: Benchmarking LLMs as Authorization Gate
abstract: Automated approval systems let coding agents execute high-risk actions with minimal human oversight by delegating the authorization decision to a classifier, typically a large language model (LLM). Such systems, adopted in tools like Claude Code and Codex, remain vulnerable to failure modes such as scope escalation, where the agent takes actions exceeding what the user authorized. Existing benchmarks focus mainly on malicious requests, evaluating refusal under an implicit policy. We introduce AuthGateBench, the first policy-guided benchmark for authorization gating under benign requests. We implement a novel pipeline where an LLM generates contrast pairs with identical action and trajectory but differing request, flipping the label between block and allow. This allows us to assess whether models reason over context rather than the action alone. We further examine whether auxiliary environment signals can help models make better decisions. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,400 instances spanning five failure modes drawn from real-world Claude Code incidents. Evaluations show accuracy degrades unevenly across failure modes as models over-rely on internal safety alignment, and models still block most actions even when explicitly authorized, revealing unstable rather than deterministic decisions; retrospectively retrieved environment signals, however, substantially improve authorization accuracy.
triage_reason: New benchmark for LLM authorization gating; a static test set without an instrument, shares L1 benchmark words only.

title: When Agents Talk, Secrets Travel: Topology-Driven Leakage and Recipient-Conditioned Sanitization in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems (MALS) introduce a privacy-leakage problem that conventional sensitivity-based defenses miss, since information disclosed to one authorized agent can propagate through routine coordination to an unauthorized one, without compromise or malicious behavior. This motivates topology-aware enforcement that blocks unauthorized propagation while preserving authorized disclosure. We evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels and measuring surface leakage and disclosure to topology-introduced recipients. We introduce RECONS, a Detect -> Decide -> Transform sanitizer conditioning intervention on recipient and execution context rather than sensitivity alone. Topology changes where protected information propagates, with disclosure to topology-introduced recipients rising from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays nearly flat at 60.6-62.8%. This effect persists across four generator models and a second orchestration framework, though magnitude and relay paths differ; framework choice separately drives a 150x leakage spread, so topology alone is not sufficient. RECONS reduces residual disclosure from 96.7% without sanitization to 29.25%, preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures versus 20.5% under blanket redaction. Detection coverage is the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 95.5% of residual disclosures. These results show that privacy enforcement in MALS must reason about the recipient and communication path realized at runtime, not sensitivity or topology assumptions alone.
triage_reason: Privacy leakage across multi-agent message topologies; shares L4's inter-agent message words but is a security defense.

title: PhysCodeGym: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Physically Verifiable 4D Reconstruction
abstract: Building physical simulations from video requires coding agents to translate observations into executable models and refine them through tool use. We introduce PhysCodeGym, a benchmark for physically verifiable 4D reconstruction with $156$ tasks covering rigid-body, liquid, deformable, and wind-driven motion. Agents autonomously inspect videos, write and run Blender programs, and revise their scenes using simulation feedback. Six metrics combine rule-based measurements with rubric-based judgments to assess visual and physical reconstruction quality. Program inspection, scene measurements, and counterfactual interventions test physical consistency under original and modified conditions. Experiments with frontier coding agents reveal a tradeoff between artifact quality and completion across reasoning-effort settings, while harness comparisons and agent traces link verification behavior with reconstruction performance. Case studies show that matching visible objects and events can coexist with physical defects. Counterfactual tests further expose latent contact and support failures in reconstructions that pass ordinary physical checks, highlighting the gap between reproducing observations and building reliable physical models. Code is available at https://github.com/ShaoShuai0605/PhysCodeGym.
triage_reason: Coding-agent benchmark for 4D reconstruction in Blender; shares L1 benchmark and L5 simulation words, not physics-engine fidelity.

title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.
triage_reason: Explicit digital-twin world model for robots; uses simulation but does not audit engine fidelity, shares L5 words only.

title: Learning Graded Sparse Mechanisms: A Representation Theorem and Certified Generalization
abstract: In a variety of multi-agent and physical environments, an element's update depends strongly on a few other elements and weakly on many, and both the identity and the number of the elements that matter change with the state of the system. Such graded sparse mechanisms are common, for instance, in flocks, crowds, learned particle simulators and the neighborhood aggregation of graph networks, yet they have received little systematic study as a class of functions with the grading given. In this paper we study the supervised learning of the mechanism when the grading is provided by the environment, as a weight on every element. First, we define the class by axioms, where each element's influence is capped by its weight, the dependence on the weights is regular, and no element is distinguished, and prove a representation theorem: the class is exactly the Lipschitz ball of a transport metric on weighted multisets, and the metric is forced by the axioms. Next, the geometry of the representation gives generalization bounds that depend on the data in two ways. One is via the sparsity profile of the data -- the law of how many elements matter and by how much -- which bounds the rate over all designs with that profile, with an exponent from the profile and no dependence on the number of elements. In a number of natural cases we also show matching lower bounds, up to constants in the exponent. The other is empirical: due to the representation result, classical empirical discrepancy bounds apply to the class as they stand, and the resulting bound is the transport distance between the two halves of the sample in the class's own metric, computed exactly by a matching, with an additional concentration term. Finally, we study a simulated Vicsek flock under four interaction rules at two noise levels, and show that the certificate is non-vacuous, a small fraction of the trivial value on every rule.
triage_reason: Learning theory for sparse particle-simulator mechanisms; shares L5's simulator words, not verification of GPU engines.

title: Large Language Model Assisted Transportation Planning through a Differentiable User Equilibrium Layer
abstract: Transportation planning has traditionally required substantial expertise in network modeling, traffic assignment, and optimization. As a result, strategic analyses such as network design, capacity expansion, and model calibration remain inaccessible to non-expert decision makers. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to bridge this gap by enabling natural-language interaction with complex transportation planning tools. However, existing LLM-based systems primarily serve as interfaces to simulation software and lack the ability to efficiently search, evaluate, and optimize transportation solutions. This study proposes an integrated human-AI transportation planning framework that combines a large language model, a model context protocol (MCP) interface, an open-source transportation planning engine (AequilibraE), and a differentiable user equilibrium (UE) assignment layer. The framework allows non-expert users to execute network analyses and improve solutions for optimization. A differentiable UE layer is developed by directly differentiating the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions of the Beckmann traffic assignment problem. The proposed framework is demonstrated through two representative planning tasks: calibration of travel time functions from observed traffic counts and network design under budget constraints. The examples illustrate how differentiable transportation models and LLM agents can jointly democratize transportation planning and substantially reduce barriers between domain expertise and transportation decision making.
triage_reason: LLM interface to transportation planning with a differentiable equilibrium layer; domain application.

title: CoverSynth: Coverage-Guided Generation of Retrieval Evaluation Sets
abstract: Enterprise agents need retrieval evaluation sets that expose domain-specific failures and guide developers towards efficient deployment tradeoffs. Neither expert-human-authored sets nor current synthetic generation methods provide a methodology for achieving the necessary coverage, reliability, efficiency, and discriminability required for such decision-making. Simultaneously, the field does not have an assessment framework for determining when an evaluation set has satisfied these properties. We introduce an evaluation set assessment framework for these criteria and CoverSynth -- a generator specifically designed to satisfy these criteria without incurring the high cost of human expert labeling. Starting from an unannotated corpus, CoverSynth targets coverage across retrieval demands and system capabilities. Deterministic checks locate evidence quotes in their sources, while model-based checks assess semantic validity to guarantee reliable ground truth. Across five public enterprise-style corpora, our method provides informative variation in difficulty, revealing unseen failure modes such as an inability of agents to handle underspecified or ambiguous requests. On the RepLiQA corpus, 91\% of human-generated queries can be answered by all members on a panel of 12 retrieval systems, compared to only 12\% of CoverSynth-generated queries. Finally, in a repeated TechQA/RepLiQA study, 12 of 12 within-harness model contrasts have positive nominal 95\% intervals on generated sets, compared with 4 of 12 on human sets. CoverSynth makes coverage and evidence quality explicit construction objectives, producing corpus-grounded evaluations that reveal retrieval headroom and differences between agent configurations.
triage_reason: Synthetic retrieval evaluation sets with a coverage framework; shares L1's evaluation words, but retrieval, no agent loop.

title: Variance-Optimal State Resampling for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards spends much of its rollout budget on states that yield no learning signal. We recast this as a question about the sampling distribution itself: under a fixed rollout budget, which distribution over states minimizes the variance of the policy-gradient estimator? The answer admits a closed-form Neyman allocation, $μ_{\mathrm{var}}^π(s) \propto d^π(s)\,σ_π(s)$, which connects naturally to GRPO's group-relative advantage and induces an emergent reverse curriculum as the policy improves, with no externally imposed schedule. Building on this principle, we propose VSR (Variance-driven State Resampling), a plug-in modification to GRPO using a prefix replay buffer and a zero-cost variance proxy. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks and long-horizon agentic tasks (Sokoban, BabyAI), VSR outperforms GRPO and GiGPO on most benchmarks with fewer generated tokens per update.
triage_reason: Neighbor: GRPO state-resampling with Neyman allocation on verifiable rewards; a new sampling recipe, kept as L2 kill-search neighbor.

title: LLM Value Functions for Credit Assignment in Agentic RL
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents remains challenging in long-horizon tasks with sparse outcome rewards, where assigning credit to individual actions is difficult. Methods such as GRPO assign the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, while critic-based methods require learning an additional value function that can be costly and unstable. We introduce LLM Value Function RL (LVRL), which uses the pretrained knowledge and in-context learning ability of an LLM to estimate policy-aware state values without finetuning a separate critic. LVRL conditions the value model on group context and calibrates its predictions using known values at the initial and terminal states, enabling step-level credit assignment from estimated value differences. We further extend this idea to learning from an expert policy through on-policy distillation (OPD), introducing LLM Value Function OPD (LVOPD), which focuses teacher supervision on actions associated with decreases in estimated value. We evaluate our approach across diverse agentic benchmarks: AppWorld, BabyAI, and SWE-bench Verified. Across policy scales (4B to 32B), LVRL consistently and substantially outperforms both GRPO and PPO. On AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified, LVRL yields absolute improvements of up to 13.6 and 8.6 percentage points over GRPO. Notably, on tasks requiring extended exploration like BabyAI, LVRL bridges the gap from total failure to 75.0% success. Furthermore, LVOPD yields consistent improvements over standard distillation baselines on AppWorld. Finally, Monte-Carlo analysis confirms that our frozen critic accurately identifies semantic pitfalls and recoveries, proving that LVRL extracts robust, policy-aware step-level credit from sparse terminal outcomes.

title: ANTE: Anticipate, Then Execute -- Learning Internal World Models for Coding Agents from Verified Beliefs
abstract: Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.
triage_reason: Coding-agent world model trained with RL; a recipe on code benchmarks, shares L2 credit words only.

title: Dynamic Conflict Clustering with Lightweight Learning and Strategic Repair for Distributed Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model distributed decision-making in multi-agent systems, where agents assign values to local variables while satisfying shared constraints. However, many DCSP solvers still rely on broad, repeated peer-to-peer communication and are largely reactive, with limited support for strategic coordination or learning. This increases communication overhead, can lead to stagnation, and reduces the success of hard instances. Hence, we propose Dynamic Conflict Clustering-Incomplete (DCC-Incomplete), a repair-based solver that combines conflict-centred decomposition, structured coordination, strategic repair, and lightweight learning for stagnation recovery. DCC-Incomplete groups the unsolved part of the problem into conflict clusters and restricts communication via a coordination layer to agents within the same conflict region. It also introduces memory-guided restart, enabling agents and clusters to pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.
triage_reason: Distributed constraint satisfaction solver; 'multi-agent' means solver nodes, shares L2's word only.

title: Recall What Is Missing: Composing Evidence from Long-Term Agent Memory
abstract: Under a limited context budget, a long-term agent must recall not merely memories that are individually relevant, but evidence that is collectively sufficient for the current query. Conventional memory access retrieves, scores, and truncates memories, often spending multiple context slots on redundant facts while leaving complementary evidence behind. We cast the read phase of long-term memory as query-conditioned evidence composition: each memory is valued by what it adds beyond the evidence already selected. We instantiate this operation with MemPursuit, a training-free mechanism that uses the residual of a sparse convex query reconstruction as a representation-space proxy for what the current memory set is missing. By reusing the query and candidate embeddings already available from retrieval, MemPursuit progressively composes nested evidence contexts without invoking a language model or cross-encoder to score each query--memory pair. The effectiveness of our method is verified on 3 popular benchmarks in comparison to strong baselines. In fixed-budget LoCoMo experiments, MemPursuit improves end-to-end accuracy by 7.2 percentage points at Top-10 and 5.5 percentage points at Top-20, with consistent gains across multiple memory frameworks, while achieving a 32.9$\times$ speedup in median reranking latency over fully batched BGE-v2-m3. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/FengQi-HITSZ/MemPursuit.
triage_reason: Embedding-space reranking for dialogue-memory QA (LoCoMo); retrieval, not a self-written lossy message; L4 words only.

title: Inverse Garment Design with Visual Agents
abstract: We study the problem of inverse garment design, reconstructing simulation-ready 3D outfits with arbitrary layers from a single image, with visual agents. Unlike differentiable optimization that is time-consuming, or feed-forward methods limited by training data, we introduce DressAgent, a hierarchical agentic system that recovers garment sewing patterns through planning and closed-loop refinement grounded in physical simulation. To this end, we first present an enhanced representation based on GarmentCode for diverse styles and arbitrary dressing layers, and build the first multi-layer sewing pattern dataset with over 15K outfits for supervision and benchmarking. Inverse design then proceeds coarse to fine: In layer planning and coarse estimation, agents infer layer order and relations, peel each layer into its own view, and estimate coarse patterns. In fine-grained refinement, an agentic trio of Tailor, Critic, and Orchestrator refines patterns in a closed loop of editing, simulating, and judging against the reference with visual and measured evidence. Carefully designed tools and an evolving memory make this refinement converge on the target geometry. We also design an agentic generation method for high-fidelity textures. DressAgent outperforms feed-forward methods by a large margin, surpasses or matches differentiable optimization in a fraction of the time, and generalizes to complex layering, diverse poses, and body shapes.
triage_reason: Garment design agent grounded in cloth simulation; shares L5's simulation word, not physics-engine fidelity.

title: When Skills Remain But Access Fails: Factorized Skill Memory for Continual Skill Internalization
abstract: Skill internalization aims to convert externally specified procedural skills into persistent model capabilities, allowing language-model agents to execute them without retrieving or reinjecting skill descriptions at inference time. Yet when new skills are learned continually, whether previously internalized skills remain usable is still poorly understood. We study forgetting in continual skill internalization and uncover a clear hierarchical structure. Early in subsequent training, a model may lose the ability to invoke an old skill from the raw request, while supplying only the correct canonical skill name substantially restores the learned behavior; with further optimization, this conditional execution also degrades. We call these two stages skill-addressing forgetting and skill-execution forgetting. Guided by this finding, we introduce Factorized Skill Memory (FSM), which separates continual skill memory into a plastic Address Memory and a stable Execution Memory. At each stage, FSM trains a new LoRA executor using only current-stage data, freezes it after acquisition, and appends it to Execution Memory; in parallel, Address Memory incrementally learns to map current requests to executors without replaying historical requests or execution trajectories. At inference time, Address Memory selects one executor from the raw request, and only that frozen executor performs a single language-model generation. On a five-stage benchmark built from 100 TaskBench skills, FSM achieves 65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% addressing accuracy across two task orders, improving over the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline by 14.3 percentage points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay, which retains historical training examples.
triage_reason: Studies forgetting across continually internalized skills in LM agents; supplies forgetting evidence to L2, L4 shares memory words.

title: The Anatomy of a Blind Spot: What an LLM Judge Must Be Shown, and How Much
abstract: Evaluation of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is increasingly delegated to LLMs acting as judges, yet what such a judge must be shown remains unresolved. We treat a judge whose reports are acted on as a regulator, in the sense of cybernetics, and ask what it must be shown, how much, in what form, and what its reports must get right. On seven public benchmarks we varied only what the judge was shown. Across three judges whose prices differ 10- to 17-fold, what the judge was shown mattered more than which judge it was. When a system revised its answers on feedback from a judge denied the material they had to respect, it ended below its starting point on instruction following and question answering. On instruction following the loss grew with each round, and it persisted when the judge saw the user's request but not the constraints and with a second judge family. On news summarisation, a correct reference summary beside the source undid most of the source's contribution, whereas on single-answer questions a reference helped. About a tenth of the source did almost all of its work, and a small entailment graph matched an LLM judge at finding errors in grounded text. We committed 83 testable clauses before running; of the 81 that ran, 32 met their bar and 50 went in the predicted direction, and most quantitative predictions from the theory failed. We report every shortfall and derive design rules tied to measured effects.
triage_reason: Shows what the judge sees matters more than which judge; supplies judge-variance evidence to L1.

title: Agent-Canary-Mas: End-to-End Evaluation of Protocol Risk in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Agent-to-agent protocols allow LLM agents to discover peers, exchange results, and coordinate tool use. A locally successful protocol attack, however, may be rejected by a later agent or propagated into a consequential task decision. Measuring local exploitability alone leaves this difference unresolved and provides limited evidence about which participant caused the final outcome. We present Agent-Canary-Mas, an end-to-end evaluation system that follows protocol risk through long-horizon multi-agent tasks. It covers five risk classes and 13 subclasses across A2A, ANP, and BCS, with 975 matched malicious--benign task pairs in five business domains. A shared OpenClaw framework runs autonomous, tool-using agents under different underlying models while preserving the task and execution setup. Matched runs separate local protocol success from downstream consequences; retained evidence connects participant selection, message consumption, tool activity, and task-state changes. We further evaluate a protocol-context Guard that checks an object's authority at consequential handoffs. Across three model conditions, local attack success is frequently at or above 90%, while consequence conversion ranges from 7.1% to 100.0%. Cross-agent evidence raises macro-averaged Audit-F1 from 29.7% to 95.5%. On Finance tasks, the Guard lowers average ASR from 86.1% to 53.8% and PTCR from 65.5% to 31.2%, with a measurable completion tradeoff. These results show that protocol risk depends on how agents use exchanged objects throughout the task, and that evaluating this path supports more informative risk assessment, attribution, and defense.
triage_reason: Security benchmark for agent-to-agent protocol attacks; shares L1 attribution words but attributes attack consequences, not outcome variance.

title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.
triage_reason: Deep-research multi-agent harness with shared workspace; a harness recipe without controlled comparison, shares L4 words only.

title: Persistent LLM Orchestration of Heterogeneous Robot Teams via Partial Delegation to Multi-Agent Protocols
abstract: Natural language specifications let non-expert users task robot teams, and large language models (LLMs) have recently proven effective at grounding such semantic specifications into plans for heterogeneous teams. Existing approaches assume missions that terminate and environments that, while unknown, do not change, but both assumptions fail in many emerging applications. For example, a disaster-response mission does not terminate, and its environment changes continuously as hazards spread and evacuees move. We identify three ways an LLM orchestrator breaks in this setting: its prompt grows without bound, its reasoning degrades as agents and targets accumulate, and it stops actively monitoring after covering the search space once. We build on the successful framework of grounded generative intelligence, and address each issue with a classical idea. A Markovian state summary, rebuilt from the semantic map at every invocation, replaces the growing interaction history. Partial delegation lets the orchestrator assign a subset of robots to an autonomous multi-agent protocol and reserve its reasoning for generating subtasks that require detailed parameters and careful ordering. Lastly, observation staleness, surfaced explicitly in the prompt, together with task-and event-triggered re-prompting, keeps the team vigilant. In a simulated urban search-and-rescue mission with spreading fire and moving evacuees, our framework rescues 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline while using six times fewer tokens. Additional ablations isolate the contribution of each mechanism.
triage_reason: LLM robot-team orchestrator with unbounded prompt; domain application, shares L4's context-growth words only.

title: Words to World: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physical Environments
abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.
triage_reason: Benchmark of LLMs controlling real robot hardware; static test set, shares L1 benchmark words, no L5 simulator question.

title: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression Ability across Large Language Models
abstract: Context compression in long-running applications of large language models (LLMs) must preserve goal-relevant information, often before specific downstream questions are known. We introduce GACC-Bench, a benchmark for Goal-Adaptive Context Compression that evaluates how reliably LLMs adapt information retention to specified high-level goals. For each source context, we derive one or more high-level goals by grouping source-grounded questions according to shared downstream objectives. The benchmark contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 document and agent-trace contexts from seven collections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. The compressor receives a source context, a goal, and a context-length budget, with the associated evaluation questions withheld. A fixed reader answers these questions individually using the same compressed context. Our evaluation of ten LLM compressors reveals substantial gaps to full-context performance even for the best-performing model, particularly in supporting correct answers to every question associated with a goal. Compared with goal-agnostic compression, target-goal conditioning consistently improves accuracy, whereas mismatched-goal conditioning reduces it. GACC-Bench is available at https://github.com/weiting24/GACC-Bench.
triage_reason: L4 measurement: goal-conditioned compression benchmark over document and agent-trace contexts with a fixed reader; a must-read for parked C-W42-02.

title: Decoupled residuals for the physics audit: count only the simulator error that no randomized parameter can reproduce
abstract: In control theory, telling a model fault apart from normal variation is solved by a residual made blind to every disturbance the model already allows, with a bank of such residuals to say which fault occurred and the alarm threshold taken from the model's own predicted spread; carried into GPU-batched robot simulation, that says the per-step physics audit should count only the part of the coarse-versus-reference one-step discrepancy that no setting of the domain-randomized physical parameters can reproduce (project out the directions in which friction, mass and actuator-gain changes move the next state at that visited state), split it per numerical knob (iteration cap, time step, contact model), and set its threshold from pure parameter-shift steps instead of from policies assumed not to exploit.
standard_answer: If a model is right, its one-step prediction errors (the innovations: what was measured minus what the model predicted one step earlier) average zero, are uncorrelated in time, and are exactly as large as the model itself predicts, so the error measured in units of that predicted spread (the normalized innovation squared, NIS) follows a chi-square law and can be tested without knowing the true state; passing is necessary but not sufficient (in Chen et al.'s example a filter with very different noise settings also averaged NIS = 2, the correct value). Fault detection turns this into a design rule: build a residual that stays exactly zero under every normal disturbance the model already allows and becomes nonzero only under a fault, and find which fault occurred with a bank of residuals, each blind to every fault but one. Such a residual exists only if the fault pushes the system in a direction that no normal disturbance can produce (Rank[H F] > Rank H); a fault that looks exactly like a normal disturbance cannot be seen by any decoupled residual.

III-A: NIS = e_z^T S^-1 e_z is chi-square with n_z degrees of freedom and 'does not require ground truth knowledge'; Sec. III-B: time-step-wise averaged NIS bounds [l_z(alpha,N), u_z(alpha,N)]; Sec. IV: a filter tuned to (0.855, 3.000, 0.122, 0.294) instead of the true (1, 2, 0.2, 0.1) also averages NIS = 2. Sec. 1 and 2.1: the residual must satisfy r(d,0) = 0 for every normal disturbance d and r(d,f) != 0 under a fault f ('decoupling unknown disturbances'); Remark 4.1: isolation is detection of one fault with the others treated as disturbances, giving a bank of filters; Fact 4.4: a decoupled fault-sensitive residual exists iff Rank[H(p) F(p)] > Rank H(p). import_sentence: In control theory, telling a model fault apart from normal variation is solved by a residual made blind to every disturbance the model already allows, with a bank of such residuals to say which fault occurred and the alarm threshold taken from the model's own predicted spread; carried into GPU-batched robot simulation, that says the per-step physics audit should count only the part of the coarse-versus-reference one-step discrepancy that no setting of the domain-randomized physical parameters can reproduce (project out the directions in which friction, mass and actuator-gain changes move the next state at that visited state), split it per numerical knob (iteration cap, time step, contact model), and set its threshold from pure parameter-shift steps instead of from policies assumed not to exploit.

predicts.statement: Definitions (glosses): domain randomization (DR) = training across simulator copies whose physical parameters theta (friction, masses, actuator gains, ...) are redrawn each episode from a range p_DR; x_t = full simulator state at step t, u_t = action, x_{t+1} = the training simulator's next state; F_ref = the same step re-simulated from x_t with more solver iterations / a smaller time step / another contact model (L5's reference); e_t = x_{t+1} - F_ref(x_t,u_t) (L5's residual, d_t = its norm); J_t = the n x K sensitivity matrix whose column j is the change in the training simulator's next state per unit change of DR parameter theta_j, from central finite differences across batched worlds reset to x_t; M = the mass matrix, so ||v||_M^2 = v^T M v is twice a kinetic energy (a coordinate-free physical norm on velocity residuals); P_perp = I - J_t (J_t^T M J_t)^-1 J_t^T M; decoupled residual r_t = P_perp e_t (the part no small change of any randomized parameter reproduces); parity share s_t = ||r_t||_M^2 / ||e_t||_M^2; floor = the same s_t computed when the 'reference' is the training simulator itself with theta shifted inside p_DR (a pure normal disturbance; nonzero only through linearization and float error); kappa_perp = 99th percentile of ||r_t|| on those floor steps (1% per-step false alarms by construction, no exploit-free policy needed); rho_perp = sum_t R_t 1[||r_t||_M > kappa_perp] / sum_t R_t with R_t the reward at step t; AUROC = probability that a random coarse-trained evaluation episode scores higher than a random fine-trained one. Measurable statement: on contact-rich tasks trained under the task's shipped DR, the exploit signal lives in the decoupled residual: rho_perp separates coarse-trained from fine-trained policies (episode-level AUROC >= 0.75, seeds as blocks) while the DR-explainable part (I - P_perp) e_t does not (AUROC <= 0.6).
predicts.expected: Ours (judgment, about 55%): on at least 2 of 3 tasks the parity share on rewarded contact steps is >= 3x the parameter-shift floor, rho_perp separates coarse from fine policies at AUROC >= 0.75, and the DR-explainable component is the larger part of d_t but does not separate them. Mechanism: an iteration-capped or large-step contact solve produces errors (energy gained on contact resolution, penetration followed by ejection) that no friction, mass or gain setting reproduces, and those are the steps where coarse-trained policies earn return; the raw d_t with one kappa mixes a large harmless component with a small exploitable one.
predicts.field_assumption: Robot-learning practice tunes solver settings until the simulation is stable and relies on DR over physical parameters to absorb what remains, i.e., it treats numerical error as a parameter shift inside the DR envelope; under that working assumption coarse- and fine-trained DR policies differ little in exploitation, and the decoupled residual carries no more signal than the raw one.
predicts.belief_changing: (a) rho_perp separates coarse from fine DR-trained policies at AUROC >= 0.75 with parity share >= 3x floor: widening DR cannot fix solver artifacts; the L5 ruler should count only decoupled residuals, and engine defaults (iteration caps, time steps) need a per-task parity check, a recipe and default change. (b) Parity share within 2x the floor on all tasks while raw d_t still separates: solver artifacts are parameter-mimicable, the fix is the DR range (an envelope check, NIS-style), and L5's 'solver artifacts are a distinct exploit class' headline is wrong.

identifiability: Random given what: in the simulator-versus-reference audit every quantity is deterministic given (x_t, u_t, theta, numerical settings), apart from GPU-batch non-determinism (atomic-add ordering, documented by GPUSimBench 2607.13059 per the L5 neighbor list). So there is no innovation noise in the Kalman sense, and the literal import (whiteness or NIS chi-square tests on d_t) is ill-posed: temporal correlation of d_t reflects the policy's visitation (a contact episode lasts many steps), not model error. That is why the import taken is the decoupling rule, not the whiteness test. The only spreads present are the protocol's DR distribution p_DR and the float floor, both measured: the float floor by stepping the identical (x_t, u_t) in two batch slots, the DR directions by J_t. Whose temperature: the policy's action sampling sets which states are visited; the audit runs the deterministic evaluation policy (mean action) and repeats under training-time sampling, since exploitation is learned under the latter; both are reported. Thing or protocol: the decomposition is a property of (engine, numerical settings, reference, DR specification) at the visited states. It is protocol-relative by design, because the question is whether this training protocol's randomization covers this artifact; the DR spec is written into the record and the result changes if DR changes. Two traps written down now: (1) J_t is undefined across contact-mode switches (a stiffness or friction perturbation changes the active contact set): central differences at two step sizes; steps where they disagree by > 50% are labelled non-smooth and reported with their return share. (2) Dimension: with K randomized parameters in an n-dimensional state, a random vector puts (n-K)/n of its energy outside the span by chance, so s_t means nothing alone; it is read only against the parameter-shift floor and in the kinetic-energy metric on object and contact-relevant coordinates.

probe.design: MuJoCo Playground on MJX (arXiv 2502.08844: open source, quadrupeds, humanoids, dexterous hands and arms, shipped sim-to-real configs, 'train policies in minutes on a single GPU'). Three contact-rich tasks with shipped DR configs: one quadruped locomotion task, one dexterous in-hand reorientation task, one arm manipulation task. For each task train coarse numerics (solver iteration cap 1, time step 2x the shipped value) and fine numerics (shipped value with iterations raised to convergence), both under the shipped DR, 3 seeds each: 18 policies. Audit 2,000 visited steps per policy: reset batched worlds to x_t and step (i) the coarse simulator at theta_0 +/- delta_j for each DR parameter at two step sizes (J_t, 4K+1 worlds), (ii) three one-knob references (more iterations only; smaller time step only; alternative contact softness only) for the per-knob residual bank, (iii) a parameter-shift null with theta drawn from p_DR for the floor and kappa_perp, (iv) a duplicate slot for the float floor. Compute raw rho (L5, kappa from fine-trained policies), rho_perp, the DR-explainable share and per-knob rho_perp^(j); 64 evaluation episodes per policy for episode-level AUROC with seeds as blocks. The same runs serve L5's own kill test 1 (does raw rho separate at all).
probe.kill_result: Dead if, on all three tasks, rho_perp separates coarse-trained from fine-trained policies no better than raw rho (episode-level AUROC difference <= 0.05), or the parity share on rewarded contact steps stays within 2x the parameter-shift floor: solver artifacts then act like parameter shifts and the raw residual with an empirical kappa already says everything (footnote worth citing: 'iteration caps behave as a friction/stiffness shift; calibrate them through DR'). Dead for a given task if > 30% of its rewarded contact steps have unstable J_t (the decomposition is not identifiable there). If neither raw rho nor rho_perp separates, L5's own kill test 1 has fired first. Costs are judgment: 18 runs at <= 3 GPU-hours each plus <= 6 GPU-hours of audit, at about $2 per GPU-hour.

papers.title: DROPO: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Offline Domain Randomization
papers.trick: Replay each real (state, action) pair in many simulator copies whose parameters are drawn from a candidate randomization distribution, fit a Gaussian to the resulting next states, and move the distribution to maximize the likelihood of the real next state.
papers.did_not_do: It treats the directions the simulator cannot produce as noise to regularize away: a small epsilon is added to the covariance diagonal 'in case singular covariance matrices would appear, e.g. due to directions of variance in the state-space unexplainable by the simulator dynamics' (Sec. 3, full text fetched). It never measures that unexplainable component, never tests the fitted envelope for consistency (no NIS bounds), compares simulation to real data rather than coarse to converged numerics, does not separate knobs, and does not weight by where a policy earns return. It even reports widening DR to 'compensate for an unmodeled phenomenon', the opposite of decoupling.

papers.title: Runtime Monitoring of Supermartingale Certificates
papers.trick: Turn each observed change of a design-time certificate value along one deployed trajectory into a bet that pays only if the certificate's expected-decrease condition is false, and alarm when the accumulated wealth crosses a level that caps the chance of ever raising a false alarm.
papers.did_not_do: It monitors one scalar certificate on a stream from the deployed system and only detects a violation. It has no decoupling from variation the model already allows, no isolation of which component is wrong, and no physics engine or RL exploitation; its benchmarks are synthetic families, Building/Tanks/LQR, and learned controller-certificate pairs (Sec. 5, full text fetched), and its stated future work is shielding and repair. Its anytime-valid betting test could replace the fixed per-step kappa, but that is a sequential-analysis (F3) mutation, not this import.

papers.title: Statistical Guarantees for Offline Domain Randomization
papers.trick: Cast offline domain randomization as maximum-likelihood fitting over a parametric simulator family and prove the fit converges to the true dynamics under identifiability and regularity conditions.
papers.did_not_do: Its guarantees assume the true dynamics lie inside the parametric family (abstract: convergence 'to the true dynamics'). It offers no test of whether a given discrepancy is inside the family, and that is exactly what the decoupled residual measures per visited step. Abstract only.

papers.title: Robust Neural Posterior Estimation and Statistical Model Criticism
papers.trick: Add an explicit error model between simulated and observed summary statistics during neural posterior estimation, so that inference is robust and the statistics the simulator cannot fit for any parameter are flagged.
papers.did_not_do: It is the simulation-based-inference version of 'find what no parameter explains', applied to scientific simulators with summary statistics. It has no per-step dynamics, no robot physics engine, no numerical-knob isolation, and no link to policy exploitation. Abstract only.

title: Rate-distortion frontier for agent compaction: already made (prompts: Nagle et al. 2024; agent compaction: Tirmazi-Bishop-Markelon-Mitzenmacher 2026 and Colaco-Lahjouji 2026); the agent residual is either headroom-versus-oracle renamed or the repeated-compaction law those two groups list as their own open problem
abstract: In information theory, a lossy message to a receiver is handled with the rate-distortion curve and the information bottleneck: keep only the bits that predict what the receiver must do, and grade every encoder by its gap to the minimum loss reachable at its length. Carried into L4, that says a compaction summary should be graded by how far the agent's downstream success after it sits below the best success any summary of the same length reaches. The import is already made: for prompts by Nagle et al. (2407.15504, an exact distortion-rate linear program); for agent compaction by Tirmazi, Bishop, Markelon and Mitzenmacher (2608.01326, minimum summary size = one-way communication complexity, with Anthropic's compaction endpoint measured at random-guess error against a Bloom-filter bound) and by Colaco and Lahjouji (2607.08032, a single compaction objective, a Fano lower bound and a repeated-compaction experiment).
standard_answer: Rate-distortion theory defines R(D), the fewest bits per symbol a lossy code must carry so that the expected distortion (the receiver's average loss) stays at or below D; the curve is monotone, no encoder can beat it, and it gives 'an analytical expression for how much compression can be achieved'. The information bottleneck removes the need to choose the distortion by hand: compress X into a code X~ by minimizing I(X~;X) - beta*I(X~;Y), where I(A;B) is mutual information (the bits A carries about B) and Y is the variable the receiver must predict, so the code keeps only the bits of X that predict Y, and when a sufficient statistic for Y exists (a summary that carries everything X says about Y) most of that information survives heavy compression. The working consequence is a ruler: plot any encoder's loss against its length beside the minimum achievable loss at that length, and the vertical gap is the part of the loss owed to the encoder rather than to the budget.

standard_answer_sources.cite: Tishby, Pereira, Bialek, 'The information bottleneck method' (2000), Sec. 2 definition of R(D) and Eq. 15 the IB functional L = I(X~;X) - beta I(X~;Y); fetched via arXiv API and PDF
Wikipedia, 'Rate-distortion theory' (introduction and definition sections; fetched through the MediaWiki API on 2026-10-18)
