predicts.statement: With the reader agent held fixed, post-compaction task success as a function of summary length is non-decreasing with diminishing returns, its knee sits near the information requirement of the facts the continuation later uses (here, the bits needed to name the files, tests and error strings the full-context continuation touches), and a production compaction prompt sits a measurable distance below the best-of-N curve at its own operating length (best-of-N: the best of N sampled summaries at the same length, picked on some continuations and scored on others).
predicts.expected: On 50 forced-compaction SWE-bench Verified histories, success stays within +/-5 pp from 512 to 4K summary tokens, because the later-used facts need roughly 10^2 bits (estimate: a few file paths and test names out of thousands) and the repository keeps the rest (judgment: 0.6). The best-of-8 summary at 2K tokens beats the mean summary by 5-10 pp under held-out scoring (judgment: 0.5), and the failures trace to missing or unsupported specific entries (cf. 2610.20927: 83% of failed runs trace to an action that carries out a summary entry, most with no supporting environment output). The loss is selection and validity, not rate.
predicts.field_assumption: Loss falls along a convex rate-distortion curve and collapses once the budget drops below the task's information requirement I*(Q) = I(Y;H|Q) (2607.08032 Eq. 2, a Fano bound: P_e >= (H(Y|Q) - B - 1)/log|Y|). More bits, or a larger compressor that packs more bits per token, buy lower loss (2512.21720's fitted rate-distortion curves).
predicts.belief_changing: Success flat across an 8x length range together with a best-of-8 gap of 10 pp or more at fixed length would say the length axis is the wrong ruler for agent compaction. The bytes-per-token budget axis proposed for COMPACT-Bench (2607.08032) and GACC-Bench's budget sweeps would then need a fixed-length selection-gap column. A steep curve with its knee within 2x of the measured information requirement would confirm 2607.08032's lens on real agents and make the budget axis the right ruler. Half of this surprise is already published: 2608.16370 reports no significant completion change at its prespecified 5x compression point in any cell, retrieval calls rising from 21.0 to 63.9 for GPT-5.5, and 'Random selection is comparable to an offline hindsight oracle'.

identifiability: Random given what: in a deterministic sandbox (SWE-bench), once the history h at the compaction point is fixed, the only randomness left comes from the compactor's sampling at temperature T_c, the reader agent's sampling at temperature T_r, and serving noise; the environment adds none. Whose temperature: the best-of-N curve exists only if the compactor is sampled at T_c > 0. A production compactor at T_c = 0 gives one summary per history, so its frontier has to come from other compactors or from search, never from resampling. Success variance after a summary is the reader's (T_r), not the compactor's. Property of what: the minimum achievable loss D*(R) belongs to the protocol (task distribution, reader model and its temperature, length unit), not to the compactor. A stronger reader lowers the whole curve, and 'full context' is not an upper bound (checklist 2026-10-16: curated memory beats raw history), so loss is measured against the best achievable summary, never against full context. Only the compactor's gap to that curve, at a fixed reader, is a property of the compactor. Bound versus achievability: the Shannon bound is in bits of the code and is vacuous here. For the success outcome, a pass/fail result carries at most 1 bit and the later-used facts about 10^2 bits (estimate), while production summaries carry about 10^4 bits (2608.01326's Opus 4.8 summaries were 13.6-14.8 kbits), so Fano gives P_e >= 0 at every operating length. Computable lower bounds exist only for synthetic query families with known communication complexity (2608.01326 used set membership). On real agent tasks, best-of-N or an oracle compaction gives an upper bound on D*(R), so the measured gap is a lower bound on the true gap: a one-sided ruler. The loss that does occur comes from computation (an LLM cannot write or read a sketch: the endpoint 'falls back to a description of the set's general character') and from not knowing the future query. Shannon information prices neither; V-information, information for a computationally limited observer (Xu et al. 2020), is the matching notion, and 2512.21720's proxy-model mutual-information estimator already approximates it. Second channel: the sandbox keeps the repository, so a summary needs only pointers, and loss shows up first as re-reading cost. The distortion measure must price tokens and tool calls, or the curve is flat by construction. Gate 0 verdict: passes only as a one-sided gap at a fixed reader under T_c > 0, which is C-W42-02's headroom measured against an oracle compaction (parked 2026-10-16).

probe.design: 50 SWE-bench Verified tasks; Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B in mini-SWE-agent; compaction forced at 32K tokens with a Codex/Claude-Code-style compaction prompt run on the same open model. At each compaction point: one summary at each of 512, 1K and 4K target tokens plus 8 summaries at 2K (T_c = 0.7); 4 reader continuations per summary (T_r = 0.7); 8 full-context continuations. That is 52 continuations per task, about 2,600 in all. Record test-pass success, tool calls and tokens to finish, the facts the full-context continuations used (files edited, test names, error strings; information requirement = log2 of the number of possible values), and the share of summary entries with no supporting environment output. Report success against length with bootstrap intervals, and best-of-8 minus mean at 2K with held-out scoring (pick on 2 continuations, score on the other 2) to remove winner's-curse bias.
probe.kill_result: Dead as a measurement residual if either (a) best-of-8 beats the mean summary at matched length by less than 5 pp under held-out scoring: there is no frontier gap to report, matching 2608.16370's random-equals-hindsight-oracle result; or (b) success rises with length, its knee falls within 2x of the information requirement, and the curve adds nothing beyond GACC-Bench-style gap-to-full-context budget sweeps. Either result is a footnote to 2607.08032 and 2608.01326 (a first rate-distortion reading of real agent compaction), not a paper.

papers.title: Context Compaction Theory (Tirmazi, Bishop, Markelon, Mitzenmacher; BU/Harvard/Proof Trading, 2026-08-02)
papers.trick: Treats the compaction summary as the single message an agent-before sends to an agent-after, proves that the smallest summary answering a family of future queries within error epsilon equals that family's one-way communication complexity (the fewest bits one party must send for the other to answer), and then scores Anthropic's compaction endpoint (Opus 4.8) against a same-size Bloom filter (a compact bit-array set-membership sketch) on 15,000-URL membership queries: error 0.505-0.555 at about 14 kbits versus about a third for the Bloom filter and 0.02 with no compaction.
papers.did_not_do: No real agent task, no tool outputs, no closed loop: one synthetic query family (set membership; 200 queries, 3 seeds) whose bound is known. Single compaction only ('We leave extending our model to a sequence of context compactions as an open problem'). Whether an LLM can attain the bound is open ('Determining which optimal budgets remain attainable ... when the interpreter is an LLM call, is an open problem'). Other query types are left open.

papers.title: What to Keep, What to Forget: A Rate-Distortion View of Memory Compaction in LLMs and Agents (Colaco, Lahjouji; UC Irvine, 2026-07-09)
papers.trick: Writes KV-cache eviction, prompt pruning, recurrent state and agent memory as one problem (minimize downstream loss subject to memory size <= B) with a Fano lower bound P_e >= (H(Y|Q) - B - 1)/log|Y| below the task's information requirement, then runs a needle-retrieval budget sweep and a repeated-summarization versus archive-retrieval experiment on Qwen2.5-1.5B (irreversible 0.33-0.56 recall versus reversible about 0.95).
papers.did_not_do: No multi-turn agent task with tool outputs (the agent reads a chunked document holding 12 key-value facts), no production compactor, and no bound computed for any agent task ('I*(Q) is never measured directly'). COMPACT-Bench is a proposal, not a release. They say the repeated compaction agents perform 'is almost never measured'.

papers.title: Fundamental Limits of Prompt Compression: A Rate-Distortion Framework for Black-Box Language Models (Nagle, Girish, Bondaschi, Makkuva, Gastpar, Kim; UT Austin/EPFL, 2024)
papers.trick: Defines the lowest answer loss reachable at each compressed-prompt length for a fixed black-box LLM as a linear program over all token-deletion compressions, solves it through its dual, and plots existing prompt compressors against that curve: a large gap, which their query-aware, variable-rate variant sometimes closes on synthetic data.
papers.did_not_do: Exact only for prompts of at most about 15 tokens ('Exactly computing the optimal rate-distortion curves for large-scale datasets, where the prompts consist of hundreds or thousands of tokens, is intractable'). The natural-language curve is a beam-search achievability approximation. Single query, no agents, no multi-turn compaction.

papers.did_not_do: 'We primarily focus on GPT-style non-reasoning models with single-round communication, limiting generalizability to reasoning-augmented models or iterative multi-agent workflows.' No compaction of tool-output histories, and the curve is fitted, not bounded.

title: Frailty or fatigue: is the falling per-minute hazard in agent time horizons a property of agents or of the task mix?
abstract: In reliability engineering, a failure rate that falls across a pooled population is solved by separating unit-to-unit frailty (some units are weak from the start) from any change in each unit's own hazard, using repeated observations that share a unit; carried into L1, that says the falling per-minute hazard fitted to METR's time-horizon data (Weibull shape about 0.6 for frontier agents and 0.37 for humans, Hamilton, January 2026) is what a task suite of fixed but unequal difficulty produces even when an agent's per-minute chance of failing on any one task never changes, and METR's 4 to 8 repeated runs per task decide which reading holds.
standard_answer: Reliability engineering describes a unit's life by its hazard rate h(t), the chance of failing in the next instant given survival so far; the Weibull model h(t) = (gamma/alpha)(t/alpha)^(gamma-1) has a shape gamma that says whether failures come early and fall off (gamma < 1, the 'infant mortality' end of the bathtub curve), arrive at a constant rate (gamma = 1, the exponential), or grow with age (gamma > 1, 'wear-out'). A falling hazard seen in a pooled population is first read as heterogeneity, called frailty (units differ in fixed quality, the weak fail early, and the survivors are stronger on average), not as each unit getting stronger with age: for any mix of constant-hazard units the pooled hazard h(t) = E[lambda e^(-lambda t)] / E[e^(-lambda t)] falls at a rate equal to the variance of the survivors' hazards, and life tables that ignore frailty are known to misstate individual aging (Vaupel, Manton and Stallard 1979; Proschan 1963 is the canonical reliability case). Before any such number is trusted, the measuring system itself is characterized by a gauge R&R study (gauge repeatability and reproducibility): the same items are re-measured in a nested design so that short-term repeatability, day-to-day reproducibility and run-to-run stability come out as separate standard deviations combined into the uncertainty of one measurement, and the automotive MSA manual calls a system whose measurement spread is under 10% of total variation adequate and over 30% unacceptable.

import_sentence: In reliability engineering, a failure rate that falls across a pooled population is solved by separating unit-to-unit frailty (some units are weak from the start) from any change in each unit's own hazard, using repeated observations that share a unit; carried into L1, that says the falling per-minute hazard fitted to METR's time-horizon data (Weibull shape about 0.6 for frontier agents and 0.37 for humans, Hamilton, January 2026) is what a task suite of fixed but unequal difficulty produces even when an agent's per-minute chance of failing on any one task never changes, and METR's 4 to 8 repeated runs per task decide which reading holds.

predicts.statement: Fit a shared-frailty Weibull to METR's per-run outcomes: run r of task i succeeds with probability exp(-z_i (t_i/theta)^k_cond), where t_i is the task's human minutes, theta a scale, k_cond the within-task hazard shape, and z_i a task multiplier with mean 1 and variance sigma^2 shared by every run of task i (sigma^2 is pinned by how often runs of the same task agree). Averaged over z_i ~ Gamma, the pooled curve is S(t) = (1 + sigma^2 (t/theta)^k_cond)^(-1/sigma^2); at sigma^2 = 1 this is exactly METR's own logistic-in-log-time curve 1/(1 + (t/theta)^k_cond), and at sigma^2 = 0 it is Hamilton's plain Weibull. So the pooled curve alone cannot separate frailty from a falling within-task hazard (Ord reports Hamilton found the two fits similar), and the run-level agreement can. Measurable statement: for most agents, k_cond is near 1 and sigma^2 is well above 0, so the falling pooled hazard comes from between-task spread.
predicts.expected: For at least 15 of 23 agents on METR-Horizon-v1.1: k_cond inside [0.8, 1.2], sigma^2 with a 95% interval above 0.3, and the frailty model at least as good as the pooled Weibull by AIC; the pooled k near 0.6 is reproduced by sigma^2 alone. Probability 0.55 (judgment). Premise for this lean: W41 counted always/never/mixed task shares on the same file (2026-10-10, unweighted, SWAA tasks included, not length-conditioned), e.g. GPT-5 0.71/0.17/0.12 of 228 tasks, i.e. runs of one task agree far more often than a shared per-length success rate allows.
predicts.field_assumption: One hazard curve is shared by all tasks of a given human length, and its shape is a property of the agent. Ord (arXiv:2505.05115): 'a constant rate of failing during each minute a human would take to do the task'; 2609.01660: 'Task success follows a geometric law governed by a single per-step reliability parameter'; 2609.19113: 'Per-round failure rates are flat across the horizon'. Hamilton (2026-01-23, updated 2026-02-03): all models have shape below 1, frontier models 'cluster between 0.6 and 0.9', humans 'approximately 0.37'; Ord (2026-02-04) reads it as 'their hazard rates systematically decline as the task goes on' and calls Hamilton probably right.
predicts.belief_changing: k_cond near 1 with large sigma^2 for most agents: the falling hazard belongs to the task suite (unequal difficulty at equal human time, plus noise in the human-minutes ruler), not to agents. Then the human-versus-agent shape gap (0.37 vs 0.6) and any 'shape improving with scale' claim compare suite heterogeneity; the 80% and 99% horizons are shares of tasks within reach, not lengths an agent can run at that reliability; and success on any single long task falls exponentially, the pessimistic tail. The opposite outcome (k_cond below 0.8 surviving the frailty term) is the first identified evidence that agents do steady within a task, and it confirms Hamilton's tail forecasts with an identification he did not have.

identifiability: Random given what: one run's success is random given (agent, scaffold, task, task_version) over the agent's own token sampling plus any environment randomness (training-run seeds in RE-Bench-style tasks); there is no simulated user and no LLM judge, since METR tasks are 'automatically scored between 0 and 1' with fixed per-task thresholds (METR paper, arXiv:2503.14499, fetched). Runs of one task are exchangeable only when scaffold and task_version match; the per-run file carries both, so the fit groups on them. Whose temperature: only the agent's. Neither the METR paper text nor the eval-analysis-public README states a sampling temperature (searched 2026-10-18). A temperature-0 agent agrees with itself by construction (up to serving noise), which inflates sigma^2 as a protocol artifact; the probe establishes each agent's sampling setting first (agent config or a question to METR) and reports sigma^2 only for agents sampled above temperature 0. Agent or protocol: k_cond and sigma^2 are properties of (agent, scaffold, task suite, human-minutes ruler), not of the agent alone. sigma^2 is the spread of task difficulty beyond human time as that agent sees it, and a multiplicative error in a task's recorded human minutes enters the model exactly as a frailty term; the per-run field human_source (baseline versus estimate) separates the two, since ruler noise predicts larger sigma^2 on estimated-time tasks (a gauge R&R reading of the x-axis). The 'time' in every published fit is the human's time on the task, a task attribute, not elapsed time in the agent's run; no within-run failure moment is observed (started_at, completed_at and tokens_count give run length, not when the fatal error happened), so 'hazard per minute' is a between-task construct in Ord's, Hamilton's and METR's fits alike. If the human curve pools different baseliners per task, person-to-person spread adds frailty that same-agent runs do not have, and the 0.37 vs 0.6 comparison is not like-for-like until both are frailty-adjusted. Identification comes from tasks near each agent's 50% horizon (tasks far shorter or longer are all-success or all-failure regardless of sigma^2), so per-agent intervals will be wide; a sigma^2 shared across agents per suite is the fallback.

Steps: (1) drop runs with fatal_error_from set; group runs by (alias, task_id, scaffold, task_version). (2) Per agent, weighted maximum likelihood for M0 exponential S = exp(-t/theta), M1 pooled Weibull S = exp(-(t/theta)^k) (first reproduce Hamilton's k as a check), and M2 shared gamma-frailty Weibull with the closed-form per-task likelihood L_i = C(n,s) * sum_{j=0}^{n-s} C(n-s,j) (-1)^j (1 + sigma^2 (s+j) (t_i/theta)^k_cond)^(-1/sigma^2) for s successes in n runs. (3) Report k_cond and sigma^2 with profile-likelihood 95% intervals, AIC against M1, and a parametric bootstrap over tasks. (4) Robustness: SWAA tasks removed; human_source = baseline only (ruler-noise check); METR's fitted logistic slope rewritten as a power of t, which is the sigma^2 = 1 reading. Do not fit before the expected result above is frozen in the seed record.

title: Lesson admission as a sequential test: an e-process gate for self-written memory, and the false-admission rate of one-success admission (already made by PACE 2606.08106)
abstract: In sequential analysis, deciding from a stream of noisy outcomes whether a change helps is solved by an e-process (a betting score) that accepts the change only when the score crosses 1/alpha, stops early either way, and holds the false-acceptance rate at alpha even when checked after every outcome; carried into L4 (self-written memory), that says a lesson should enter an agent's playbook only after paired with-versus-without task outcomes push its e-process past 1/alpha, so an agent that admits a lesson on its own judgment or after one success runs this test with no error control (alpha effectively 1) and its false-admission rate is a number computable from paired logs.
standard_answer: Sequential analysis tests a hypothesis while the data arrive: an e-process is a running betting score that starts at 1 and, when the null hypothesis (here, 'this change does not help') is true, behaves like the wealth of a gambler in a fair game, so it seldom grows large. Ville's inequality bounds the chance that such a score ever reaches 1/alpha by alpha, so rejecting the null the first time the score crosses 1/alpha keeps the false-rejection rate at alpha at every stopping time, including stopping because the data looked good (optional stopping, the 'peeking' that breaks an ordinary p-value). Confidence sequences are the estimation version, intervals that hold at all times at once and generalize Wald's sequential probability ratio test (SPRT: two fixed hypotheses, stopping rule set in advance by the target error rates) to nonparametric settings, so a comparison ends as soon as its evidence is decisive instead of at a sample size fixed beforehand.

Game-theoretic statistics and safe anytime-valid inference. arXiv 2210.01948 (2022); abstract plus Sec. 2.5 (Ville's inequality, Eq. 9: sup_P P(exists t: E_t >= 1/alpha) <= alpha) and Sec. 2.6 (sequential test = reject the first time the e-process reaches 1/alpha; contrast with Wald's tests) read in the PDF

Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe, Sekhon. Time-uniform, nonparametric, nonasymptotic confidence sequences. arXiv 1810.08240 (2018); abstract: confidence sequences 'generalize [the SPRT] to nonparametric settings'

predicts.statement: On a stream of candidate lessons with paired with/without outcomes, the false-admission rate (share of admitted lessons whose true effect on task success is zero or negative) of one-success or self-judged admission is large, and a per-lesson e-process gate at alpha = 0.05 holds it at or below 0.05 under peeking; the measurable residual is how many lesson-sized effects such a gate can decide within a deployment practice budget.
predicts.expected: At single-lesson grain on deterministic sandboxes (ALFWorld, AppWorld, WebShop) the e-process decides (crosses 1/alpha or stops for futility) for under 10% of lessons within 600 paired episodes, because RBC reports 'a single lesson rarely moves success beyond the noise of a few hundred episodes'; the gate's value at this grain is refusal, not selection, and the false-admission rate of admit-everything is above one half (judgment, probability 0.6).
predicts.field_assumption: The field assumes effects large enough relative to noise that an anytime-valid test stops early on average and saves budget: PACE reports about 18% lower evaluation cost than greedy acceptance at matched held-out accuracy; AV-AIVAT stops at a median 74x fewer hands after variance reduction.
predicts.belief_changing: If a majority of single lessons are decided within 300 paired episodes, lesson-grain admission is affordable and RBC's hand-chosen block grouping is unnecessary; if under 10% are decided within 600, every per-lesson gate (one success, self-judge, keep-better held-out) chooses by noise at deployment budgets and block size should be set by the e-process's expected stopping time. Both halves are already printed in substance: PACE (greedy commits 30-42% false edits, 72-100% false when no real gain exists), SAGE (naive-gate regression rate 36.5% to 0% on LiveMath, 42.8% to 0% on OfficeQA), ADMITOR (execution-success admission precision 0.726, i.e. 27% false admissions) and RBC (blocks chosen because single lessons sit under the noise floor).

identifiability: Random given the task draw and the actor's own sampling. In ALFWorld, AppWorld and WebShop the environment is deterministic after the action (RSE-Bench: 'the same action sequence yields the same verdict'), so a lucky success is the actor's sampling at its temperature (RBC protocol: actors at 0.7, Reflector and Curator at 0) plus which task was drawn; there is no environment luck term. The tested quantity, a fixed lesson's mean effect on success over the task distribution with the actor at its serving temperature, is a property of (lesson text, actor model, actor temperature, task distribution); the reflector's temperature does not enter because the lesson text is held fixed while it is tested. The false-admission rate is a property of the gate protocol (alpha, sample, whether it peeks), not of the agent; Gate 0 passes on that reading. At actor temperature 0 each task's outcome is fixed up to serving noise, so the test must sample tasks, not reruns. Verifier versus judge: on these benchmarks the outcome is the environment's verifier; in SkillOS and ReasoningBank it is an LLM judge (about 72.7% accurate in ReasoningBank's calibration), which adds judge error the e-process would absorb as outcome noise.
